newsitem.title: USA: Clinton proposes drug testing for driver's licenses.
newsitem.headline: Clinton proposes drug testing for driver's licenses.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Saturday proposed requiring teenagers to pass a drug test to get a driver's license and he unveiled a federal rule that would take away their permits if they drink and drive.

Clinton said in his weekly radio address he has ordered Transportation Secretary Federico Pena and drug czar Barry McCaffrey to study ways to make drug testing a mandatory part of the high school ritual of getting a driver's license.
The two have been asked to report back to him within 90 days on the issue, including on whether passing legislation would be necessary.

He also hailed next week's implementation of a law passed last year to require states to take away driver's licenses from teenagers who are caught drinking and driving or to risk losing their federal highway funds.

"I believe we should use the privilege of a driver's license to demand responsible behaviour by young people when it comes to drugs too," Clinton said in a transcript of the address released by the White House.

"We're already saying to teens, if you drink you aren't allowed to drive. Now we should say that teens should pass a drug test as a condition of getting a driver's license," he said. "Our message should be simple: no drugs or no driver's license."

Clinton asked Pena and McCaffrey to look into many issues, including drug testing for minors applying for permits and revoking driving licenses of people caught driving under the influence of drugs or as a sanction for other drug offences.

Clinton has made the fight against teenage drug use and youth crime regular themes in this election year, exhorting young people not to take drugs and championing ideas like school uniforms to cut down on school violence.
The issue of teenage drinking and driving was one that he spoke to last year, calling in a June, 1995, radio address for Congress to pass legislation for a "zero tolerance" policy.

The federal rule that Clinton unveiled, which formally goes into effect on Monday, implements the resulting law by requiring states to make it illegal for anyone under the age of 21 to drive with alcohol in their bloodstream and to punish them by suspending their driver's licenses if they do.

For the purpose of the law, the maximum amount of alcohol permissible in the bloodstream would be 0.02 percent. A White House official said that this would allow for the presence of "trace" amounts, for example from using mouthwash.
In most states, drunk driving is defined as a blood alcohol content of 0.1 percent.

The law requires states to put such laws in effect within two years, saying those that do not adopt such a policy would risk losing five percent of their federal highway construction funds in the first year and 10 percent each year thereafter.

Clinton was expected to rest on Saturday before heading off on a four-day campaign trip to New York, New Jersey, Ohio, Michigan and Florida starting Sunday. Two and a half weeks from the Nov. 5 election, Clinton leads his opponent Republican Bob Dole by double digits, according to most national opinon polls.
